note: Interview prep bank (FR-50, handoff 12l). Open questions are the Practice bank's (src/content/practice-questions.json), with "a strong answer covers" taken from its lookFor; never written by the model. Choice questions are for the timed test, hand-written by Development on 2026-10-20 and not yet checked by someone who works in the role: reviewed is false until they are, and production shows only reviewed ones. Follow-ups on open questions (docs/plans/mock-followups-plan.md) are Development's own too, one or two for every open question: followUpsReviewed is false until someone who works in the role checks them, and production asks only reviewed ones.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself and why you are applying for this role.
questions.strongCovers: A clear two-minute story from education to current work to this role, without reading out the resume.

followUps.text: Say which one thing from your studies or work you would use in this role in your first month.
Name one part of this role you still need to learn, and how you are learning it now.

questions.question: Describe a time you had to explain a technical issue to someone without a technical background.
questions.strongCovers: Plain words, checking the listener understood, and an outcome rather than jargon.

followUps.text: How did you check that they had understood, rather than only nodding along?
What did they decide or do differently once they understood?

questions.question: How would you write a status update to your manager when a task is going to miss its deadline?
questions.strongCovers: Early warning, the reason, the new date and what help is needed, kept short.

followUps.text: Say when you would send it: the day you see the risk, or the day before the deadline, and why.
What would you ask your manager for in that update, if anything?

questions.question: Tell me about a disagreement with a teammate and how you handled it.
questions.strongCovers: Listening, staying on facts, and a resolution that kept the working relationship.

followUps.text: Looking back, what would you do differently the next time you disagree with someone on your team?

questions.question: How do you make sure you have understood a task correctly before starting it?
questions.strongCovers: Asking clarifying questions, restating the ask and confirming the expected output.

followUps.text: Say what you would do if the person who gave the task is busy and you can't reach them.
How would you write down what you agreed, so nobody remembers it differently later?

questions.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python, and when would you use each?
questions.strongCovers: Mutability, tuples as fixed records or dict keys, and a sensible example.

followUps.text: Give a case where a tuple works as a dictionary key and a list would not.
If a function gets a list and changes it, what does the code that called it see afterwards?

questions.question: How would you read a large CSV file in Python without loading it all into memory?
questions.strongCovers: Iterating line by line or with csv.reader, generators, or chunked reading in pandas.

followUps.text: Say how you would add up one column across the whole file while reading it in pieces.
What would you do with rows that fail to parse halfway through the file?

questions.question: Explain how exceptions work in Python and how you would handle a failed API call.
questions.strongCovers: try/except with specific exceptions, retries or logging, and not swallowing errors silently.

followUps.text: How many times would you retry the call, and how long would you wait between tries?
What would you write to the log when the call finally fails, and what would you leave out?

questions.question: What is a virtual environment and why do you use one?
questions.strongCovers: Isolating project dependencies and pinning versions in requirements.txt or similar.

followUps.text: Say how a teammate would set up the same package versions on their laptop from your project.
What would you do if two packages need different versions of the same library?

questions.question: Write a function that returns the count of each word in a sentence.
questions.strongCovers: A dict or collections.Counter, handling case and punctuation, and clean readable code.

followUps.text: How would your function treat "Data" and "data," with a comma: as one word or two?
Say how you would return only the three most common words.

questions.question: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
questions.strongCovers: Unmatched rows kept on the left side with NULLs, explained with a small example.

followUps.text: With a customers table and an orders table, which join finds customers who have never ordered, and how do you pick them out?
What happens to your row count when one customer has three orders?

questions.question: How would you find duplicate email addresses in a customers table?
questions.strongCovers: GROUP BY with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, and how to see the full duplicate rows.

followUps.text: Would the same email typed with capital letters or a trailing space count as a duplicate in your query?
Once you have found the duplicates, how would you decide which row to keep?

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.strongCovers: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

followUps.text: Give one query that uses both: only this year's orders, then only regions with more than 100 of them.
Which of the two can use an index on the filtered column, and why does that matter on a big table?

questions.question: Write a query to get the second highest salary from an employees table.
questions.strongCovers: A correct approach using ORDER BY with OFFSET, a subquery or a window function, and handling ties.

followUps.text: What does your query return if two people tie for first place?
How would you change it to get the second highest in each department?

questions.question: What is an index and when can it slow things down?
questions.strongCovers: Faster reads on filtered columns, slower writes and extra storage, and not indexing everything.

followUps.text: Say how you would check whether a slow query actually uses the index.
A payments table gets thousands of inserts a minute. Which columns would you index there, and which not?

questions.question: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
questions.strongCovers: Merge keeps history with a merge commit, rebase rewrites it linearly, and not rebasing shared branches.

followUps.text: Say why you would not rebase a branch your teammates have already pulled.
Which do you use to bring main into your feature branch before a pull request, and why?

questions.question: How do you resolve a merge conflict?
questions.strongCovers: Reading both sides, editing the file, testing, then adding and committing the result.

followUps.text: How do you check that the merged file still works before you commit it?
When would you ask the teammate who wrote the other side before choosing?

questions.question: What would you do if you committed a file containing a password by mistake?
questions.strongCovers: Rotate the secret first, then remove it from history, and add the file to .gitignore.

followUps.text: If the commit is already pushed, what do you do first, before cleaning the history?
How would you stop the same mistake happening next time?

questions.question: Describe the branching workflow you have used in a team.
questions.strongCovers: Feature branches, pull requests with review, and how releases or hotfixes were handled.

followUps.text: Say how an urgent fix reached production in that workflow while a release was half done.
What did a pull request need before it could be merged in your team?

questions.question: What does git stash do and when would you use it?
questions.strongCovers: Saving uncommitted work temporarily to switch tasks, then applying it back.

followUps.text: Say how you get the stashed work back, and what happens if it clashes with your new changes.
When would you make a quick commit on your branch instead of stashing?

questions.question: What are the common HTTP methods and when do you use each?
questions.strongCovers: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE matched to read, create, replace, update and delete, with idempotency.

followUps.text: Which of these methods are idempotent, and why does that matter when a mobile app retries on a poor network?
When would you use PATCH rather than PUT to update a user's profile?

questions.question: What do the status codes 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 500 mean?
questions.strongCovers: Correct meanings, especially the difference between 401 and 403.

followUps.text: Give one request that should get 401 and one that should get 403.
Your API returns 200 with an error message inside the body. What problem does that cause for the app calling it?

questions.question: How would you design the endpoints for a simple to-do list API?
questions.strongCovers: Resource-based URLs, correct methods, status codes and a sensible request and response shape.

followUps.text: What should the API return when someone asks for a to-do item that belongs to another user?
How would you let the app fetch only the items not done yet?

questions.question: How do you handle pagination in an API that returns thousands of records?
questions.strongCovers: Limit and offset or cursor-based pagination, and the trade-offs between them.

followUps.text: Say what goes wrong with offset paging when new records are added while someone scrolls.
What would your response include so the app knows there is a next page?

questions.question: How would you secure a REST API?
questions.strongCovers: HTTPS, authentication such as tokens, authorisation checks, input validation and rate limiting.

followUps.text: How would the API reject a token that has expired or been revoked?
What would you log for each request so misuse can be traced later, without logging passwords or tokens?

questions.question: How do you handle a stakeholder who keeps changing requirements mid-sprint?
questions.strongCovers: Making the impact visible, a change process, and agreeing priorities rather than silently absorbing work.

followUps.text: Say what you would do if the stakeholder insists the change can't wait for the next sprint.
How would you stop the same thing happening again next sprint?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to say no to a senior stakeholder.
questions.strongCovers: A respectful no backed by data, with an alternative offered.

followUps.text: What did you offer them instead of a plain no?
How did the working relationship go after that?

questions.question: How do you keep business and technical teams aligned on a project?
questions.strongCovers: Regular updates, shared written scope, and one owner for decisions.

followUps.text: Say what you would do when the two teams read the same written scope in different ways.

questions.question: How do you decide when two stakeholders want conflicting things?
questions.strongCovers: Linking each ask to business goals, involving the decision owner and documenting the choice.

followUps.text: Say who makes the final call when the two can't agree, and how you would bring it to them.
How would you tell the stakeholder whose ask lost?

questions.question: How do you communicate a delay to a client?
questions.strongCovers: Telling them early and honestly, with the cause, the new plan and what is being done to recover.

followUps.text: Say what you would do if the client is angry and asks who is to blame.
What would you send them in writing after the call?

questions.question: What is the difference between EC2, Lambda and ECS, and when would you choose each?
questions.strongCovers: Servers versus functions versus containers, matched to workload, cost and control.

followUps.text: A job runs for 40 minutes every night. Which would you pick, and why not Lambda?
How would cost guide your choice for a small app with very little traffic?

questions.question: How would you give an EC2 instance access to an S3 bucket securely?
questions.strongCovers: An IAM role on the instance with least privilege, not access keys stored on the server.

followUps.text: Say what the role's policy would allow: which actions, on which bucket.
Why is keeping access keys on the server a risk, even on a private instance?

questions.question: What is a VPC and what are public and private subnets?
questions.strongCovers: Network isolation, internet gateway for public subnets, NAT for private subnets reaching out.

followUps.text: Where would you put the database, and how would the app servers reach it?
How does a server in a private subnet download updates from the internet?

questions.question: How would you make a web application on AWS highly available?
questions.strongCovers: Multiple availability zones, a load balancer, auto scaling and a managed database with failover.

followUps.text: What happens to your users if one availability zone goes down, and how would you know it works?
Where would you keep user sessions so any server behind the load balancer can serve a user?

questions.question: How do you keep an eye on AWS costs?
questions.strongCovers: Budgets and alerts, Cost Explorer, tagging, right-sizing and stopping unused resources.

followUps.text: Say what you would do the morning a budget alert says spend is double last month's.
How would tags help you tell which team or project is spending the money?

questions.question: How do you check which process is using the most CPU or memory on a Linux server?
questions.strongCovers: top or htop, ps with sorting, and what to do next.

followUps.text: The top process is your own app. Say what you would check next before restarting it.
How would you tell a short spike from a load that has stayed high for hours?

questions.question: What do file permissions like 755 and 644 mean?
questions.strongCovers: Owner, group and others with read, write and execute, and when to use each.

followUps.text: What permissions would you give a shell script, and what a config file that holds a password?
Say why 777 is a bad idea on a shared server.

questions.question: How would you find what is using the space when a server's disk is full?
questions.strongCovers: df to find the filesystem, du to find large folders, and checking logs before deleting.

followUps.text: The biggest file is a log that is still being written. Say what you do with it instead of deleting it.
df shows the disk full but du can't find the files. What could be holding the space?

questions.question: How would you find all lines containing ERROR in a log file and count them?
questions.strongCovers: grep with -c or a pipe to wc -l, and tail -f for live logs.

followUps.text: How would you count only today's ERROR lines?
How would you see which error message appears most often?

questions.question: How do you check whether a service is running and restart it?
questions.strongCovers: systemctl status and restart, and journalctl to read why it failed.

followUps.text: The service keeps failing after a restart. Say what you would read, and what you would look for.
How would you make sure the service starts again after the server reboots?

questions.question: What is the difference between a resource group and a subscription in Azure?
questions.strongCovers: Subscription as the billing and access boundary, resource groups as logical containers inside it.

followUps.text: Say how you would group the resources for a test and a production setup of one app.
What happens to the resources inside when you delete a resource group?

questions.question: How would you give an application access to Azure resources without storing a password?
questions.strongCovers: A managed identity with role-based access, and Key Vault for any secrets.

followUps.text: Say the difference between a system-assigned and a user-assigned managed identity, and when you would pick each.
Where would the app keep a third-party API key, such as one for an SMS provider?

questions.question: What is the difference between Azure VMs, App Service and Azure Functions?
questions.strongCovers: Infrastructure versus managed web hosting versus serverless, with a fitting use case for each.

followUps.text: A small company wants a website plus a job that resizes uploaded photos. Which would you use for each?
When would cold starts on Azure Functions be a problem for users?

questions.question: What is Microsoft Entra ID used for?
questions.strongCovers: Identity and access management, users and groups, single sign-on and conditional access.

followUps.text: Give an example of a conditional access rule you would set for staff signing in from outside the office.
How does single sign-on help when someone leaves the company?

questions.question: How would you control who can do what in an Azure subscription?
questions.strongCovers: Azure RBAC with built-in roles at the right scope and least privilege.

followUps.text: At which scope would you give a developer access to only their team's resources?
How would you check who has Owner rights on the subscription, and how often?

questions.question: What is the difference between Compute Engine, App Engine, Cloud Run and GKE?
questions.strongCovers: VMs, managed apps, serverless containers and managed Kubernetes, with when to use each.

followUps.text: An API with uneven traffic that drops to nothing at night: which would you pick, and why?
When is GKE worth the extra work over Cloud Run?

questions.question: How do service accounts work in Google Cloud?
questions.strongCovers: Identities for workloads, granted IAM roles with least privilege, and avoiding downloaded keys.

followUps.text: Why would you avoid downloading a key file for a service account, and what would you use instead?
Say which roles you would give a service account that only reads from one bucket.

questions.question: How is a Google Cloud project used to organise resources?
questions.strongCovers: Projects as the unit for billing, APIs and access, grouped under folders and an organisation.

followUps.text: Say how you would split projects for test and production, and why.
How would you see the bill for each project or team?

questions.question: What is BigQuery and how is it billed?
questions.strongCovers: Serverless data warehouse, paying for storage and data scanned, and using partitions to cut cost.

followUps.text: A query scans 2 TB every time someone opens a dashboard. Say how you would cut that.
Why does SELECT * cost more in BigQuery than naming the columns?

questions.question: How would you store files that the public can download from Google Cloud?
questions.strongCovers: Cloud Storage buckets with careful access settings or signed URLs, not making everything public.

followUps.text: If only paying customers should download a file, how would you give them a link that stops working later?
How would you serve the files quickly to users across India?

questions.question: How would you design a URL shortener?
questions.strongCovers: Generating short keys, a data store, handling redirects at scale and caching popular links.

followUps.text: Two people shorten different links at the same moment. Say how you make sure they never get the same short code.
Would you use a 301 or a 302 redirect, and what does that change for counting clicks?

questions.question: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
questions.strongCovers: Adding machines versus bigger machines, with limits and trade-offs of each.

followUps.text: Your app's database is on one big server that is nearly maxed out. Say what you would do first.
What has to change in an app before you can put more servers behind it?

questions.question: When would you add a cache to a system and what problems can it cause?
questions.strongCovers: Faster reads for hot data, plus stale data, invalidation and cache misses.

followUps.text: A product's price changes but users still see the old price. Say how you would stop that.
What happens to the database when the cache restarts empty in the middle of a festive sale?

questions.question: How would you design a system to send OTP messages to millions of users?
questions.strongCovers: A queue, retries, rate limits, provider failover and expiry of the codes.

followUps.text: The SMS provider goes down during a festive sale. Say what your system does.
How would you stop one person asking for fifty OTPs in a minute?

questions.question: What is a load balancer and why is it needed?
questions.strongCovers: Spreading traffic across servers, health checks and removing a single point of failure.

followUps.text: How does the load balancer know a server is unhealthy, and what does it do then?
With one load balancer, isn't that a new single point of failure? How is that handled?

questions.question: What is Terraform state and why does it matter?
questions.strongCovers: State maps code to real resources, kept in a remote backend with locking, never edited by hand.

followUps.text: Two engineers run apply at the same time. Say what stops them breaking the state.
Why should the state file not go into Git?

questions.question: What is the difference between terraform plan and terraform apply?
questions.strongCovers: Plan previews changes and apply makes them, with plans reviewed before applying.

followUps.text: The plan shows a database will be destroyed and created again. Say what you would do before applying.
How would a team review plans before anyone runs apply?

questions.question: How do you reuse Terraform code across environments?
questions.strongCovers: Modules with variables, and separate state per environment.

followUps.text: Say how you would keep a module change from reaching production before it is tested in staging.
Where would the different values for test and production live?

questions.question: How do you keep secrets out of Terraform code?
questions.strongCovers: Variables from a secrets manager or environment, marking them sensitive, and not committing tfvars with secrets.

followUps.text: Even when a variable is marked sensitive, where can the secret still show up?
Say how the pipeline would pass the database password to Terraform.

questions.question: How does Terraform handle a resource that someone changed manually in the console?
questions.strongCovers: Drift shows in the next plan, and the fix is to update code or re-apply rather than leave it.

followUps.text: Say how you would find out who made the manual change and why.
How would you stop people changing these resources by hand in future?

questions.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
questions.strongCovers: Image as the read-only template, container as a running instance of it.

followUps.text: If you change a file inside a running container, what happens to the image?
How would you run two containers from the same image with different settings?

questions.question: How would you make a Docker image smaller?
questions.strongCovers: Slim base images, multi-stage builds, fewer layers and a .dockerignore file.

followUps.text: Say what a multi-stage build leaves out of the final image for a Java or Node app.
How does the order of lines in a Dockerfile change how long a rebuild takes?

questions.question: How do containers talk to each other in Docker Compose?
questions.strongCovers: A shared network where services reach each other by service name.

followUps.text: Your app container starts before the database is ready and fails. What would you do?
How would you stop the database port being open to the outside?

questions.question: How do you keep data when a container is removed?
questions.strongCovers: Volumes or bind mounts, not writing important data inside the container layer.

followUps.text: When would you pick a named volume over a bind mount?
Say how you would back up the data in a database volume.

questions.question: How would you debug a container that exits right after starting?
questions.strongCovers: docker logs, checking the command and entrypoint, and running it interactively.

followUps.text: The logs are empty. Say what you would try next.
How would you check whether the container was killed for using too much memory?

questions.question: What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
questions.strongCovers: Automatic build and test, ready-to-release builds, and automatic release to production.

followUps.text: Which of the three would you choose for a banking app, and why?
What has to be true about your tests before continuous deployment is safe?

questions.question: What stages would you put in a pipeline for a web application?
questions.strongCovers: Build, unit tests, linting or security scans, packaging, deploy to staging, then production.

followUps.text: Which stage would you run first to give developers the quickest answer, and why?
Who or what decides that a build goes from staging to production?

questions.question: How do you store secrets used by a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.strongCovers: The CI tool's secret store or a vault, never in the repository or logs.

followUps.text: How would you stop a secret being printed in the build logs?
Say what you would do if a pipeline secret leaked.

questions.question: How should a pipeline help you recover when a deployment breaks production?
questions.strongCovers: Quick rollback to the last good version, and smaller, frequent releases to limit risk.

followUps.text: Say how you would decide between rolling back and pushing a fix forward.
What about a database change that can't simply be rolled back?

questions.question: How would you stop broken code from being merged to the main branch?
questions.strongCovers: Required checks and reviews on pull requests, with branch protection rules.

followUps.text: Say what you would do when a check fails only sometimes and the team starts ignoring it.
Who should be able to merge without the checks passing, if anyone?

questions.question: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
questions.strongCovers: Untrusted input changing a query, prevented with parameterised queries and input validation.

followUps.text: Parameterised queries can't hold a column name. Say how you would handle a sort column the user picks.
How would you look for SQL injection in a codebase you have just joined?

questions.question: What is cross-site scripting and how do you prevent it?
questions.strongCovers: Injected scripts in pages, prevented by output encoding, input checks and a content security policy.

followUps.text: Say how stored XSS differs from reflected XSS, with an example of each.
What would your content security policy allow, and what would it block?

questions.question: Name a few items from the OWASP Top 10 and explain one in detail.
questions.strongCovers: Correct items such as broken access control, with a clear real-world example and fix.

followUps.text: Say how you would test for the one you explained in an app you are given access to.
Which fix would you ask the team to do first, and how would you explain the risk to a product manager?

questions.question: How should passwords be stored in a database?
questions.strongCovers: Salted hashes with a slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2, never plain text or simple hashes.

followUps.text: Why is a fast hash such as SHA-256 a poor choice for passwords?
Say what you would do with old MD5 hashes when moving users to bcrypt.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
questions.strongCovers: Who you are versus what you can do, with an example of each failing.

followUps.text: Give an example from a shopping app where authentication works but authorisation fails.
Where in the code should the authorisation check live so it can't be skipped?

questions.question: Your manager says average order value went up this month. What would you check before agreeing?
questions.strongCovers: Looking at the median and the spread, outliers and sample size, not just the mean.

followUps.text: One customer placed a ₹5 lakh bulk order this month. Say how that changes what you tell your manager.
How many orders would you want to see before trusting the change?

questions.question: How would you explain a p-value to a sales manager with no statistics background?
questions.strongCovers: Plain words about how surprising the result would be by chance, without overclaiming.

followUps.text: The manager asks, "So there is a 95% chance the new offer works?" What do you say?
When would you tell them a significant result is still too small to matter?

questions.question: When would you report the median instead of the average?
questions.strongCovers: Skewed data such as salaries or order values, with a concrete example.

followUps.text: Give an example from your own work or studies where the average told the wrong story.
Would you ever show both, and how would you label them for a reader who isn't technical?

questions.question: Two campaigns had conversion rates of 3.1% and 3.4%. How would you decide if the difference is real?
questions.strongCovers: Sample sizes, a significance test or confidence interval, and practical importance.

followUps.text: What would you need to know to work out how many visitors each campaign needs?
If the gap is real, how would you decide whether it is worth moving budget to the better campaign?

questions.question: What is the difference between correlation and causation, with an example from business data?
questions.strongCovers: A realistic example and what extra evidence would be needed to claim cause.

followUps.text: Say what third factor could explain your example instead.
How would you test whether one actually causes the other?

questions.question: You receive a customer file with duplicate rows and missing phone numbers. How do you clean it?
questions.strongCovers: A clear order of steps: define a duplicate, decide how to treat blanks, and keep a record of changes.

followUps.text: Two rows have the same name and city but different phone numbers. Are they duplicates? How do you decide?
Say how you would record what you changed so someone else can check it later.

questions.question: Dates in a sheet come in three different formats. How would you fix them?
questions.strongCovers: Detecting each format, converting to one standard, and checking rows that fail.

followUps.text: How would you tell whether 03/04/2025 means 3 April or 4 March?
What would you do with the rows that still fail to convert?

questions.question: How do you decide whether to drop, fill or flag missing values?
questions.strongCovers: Reasoning from how much is missing, why it is missing and what the analysis needs.

followUps.text: Delivery time is missing far more often for one city than the others. Say what you would do.
How would you tell the reader of your report what you did with the missing values?

questions.question: City names are spelt differently across rows, such as Bengaluru and Bangalore. What would you do?
questions.strongCovers: A mapping table or rules, applied consistently, and a check for new variants.

followUps.text: Next month a new spelling, "B'lore", turns up. Say how your process catches it.
Where would you keep the mapping so the next analyst can reuse it?

questions.question: How do you check that your cleaning didn't change the totals you report?
questions.strongCovers: Row counts and key totals compared before and after, with reasons for any difference.

followUps.text: The row count dropped by 200 after cleaning. Say how you would explain that to your manager.
Which totals would you compare for a sales file, and against what?

questions.question: A manager wants to see monthly sales by region. Which chart would you use, and why?
questions.strongCovers: Picking a chart for the question, such as lines over time, and keeping it readable.

followUps.text: There are 12 regions. Say how you would keep the chart readable.
How would you show whether each region met its target?

questions.question: When is a pie chart a poor choice?
questions.strongCovers: Many categories or close values, and a better alternative such as a sorted bar chart.

followUps.text: A manager insists on a pie chart for 10 product categories. What would you do?
When, if ever, is a pie chart the right choice?

questions.question: How would you design a dashboard for a store manager who has two minutes each morning?
questions.strongCovers: The few numbers that matter first, clear labels, and detail only on demand.

followUps.text: Say which three numbers you would put at the top, and why those.
How would the manager see at a glance that something needs attention today?

questions.question: Tell me about a chart you made that changed someone's decision.
questions.strongCovers: A specific situation, the choice of chart, and the decision it led to.

followUps.text: What did the person decide to do differently after seeing it?
If you made it again, what would you change about the chart?

questions.question: How do you avoid a chart that misleads?
questions.strongCovers: Honest axes, consistent scales, clear labels and context such as targets or last year.

followUps.text: When is it fine for a y-axis not to start at zero?
Say how you would get someone to check your chart before it goes to senior managers.

questions.question: How would you combine two sheets that share a customer ID?
questions.strongCovers: XLOOKUP or INDEX-MATCH, handling IDs that don't match, and checking the result.

followUps.text: Some IDs are in only one sheet. Say how you would find and report them.
How would you check that the combined sheet has the right number of rows?

questions.question: Walk me through building a pivot table to show sales by month and product.
questions.strongCovers: Clean source data, the right rows, columns and values, and grouping dates.

followUps.text: Say what you would fix in the source data before making the pivot.
Next month new rows are added. How does the pivot pick them up?

questions.question: A formula returns #N/A for some rows. How do you find out why?
questions.strongCovers: Checking for extra spaces, data types and missing keys before hiding errors.

followUps.text: The ID looks the same in both sheets but still gives #N/A. What would you check?
Why might wrapping the formula in IFERROR hide a real problem?

questions.question: How would you make a monthly report in Excel quicker to update next time?
questions.strongCovers: Tables, named ranges or Power Query, and fewer manual copy-paste steps.

followUps.text: Say which manual step in the report you would remove first, and how.
How would a teammate update the report without having to ask you?

questions.question: What checks do you do before sending a spreadsheet to your manager?
questions.strongCovers: Totals cross-checked, formulas not broken, clear labels and no hidden mistakes.

followUps.text: Say how you would cross-check a total against the source before sending.
What would you write in the email with the file so your manager reads it correctly?

questions.question: Which clause filters groups after GROUP BY?
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups after the rows are grouped and counted. WHERE filters single rows before grouping.

questions.question: A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders returns…
options: Every customer, with empty order columns where there is no order
Only orders that have a customer
Every pairing of every customer with every order
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills the right table's columns with NULL where nothing matches.

questions.question: What does COUNT(column) leave out?
questions.explanation: COUNT(column) counts the rows where that column is not NULL. COUNT(*) counts every row.

questions.question: Which keyword removes repeated rows from a query's result?
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT returns each different row once. UNIQUE is a constraint on a table, not part of a SELECT.

questions.question: What does len({1, 2, 2, 3}) return?
questions.explanation: Curly braces with values make a set, and a set keeps one copy of each value: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.question: Which of these can be a dictionary key?
options: A tuple of numbers, such as (1, 2)
questions.explanation: Keys must be hashable, which means they cannot change. Tuples of numbers can't change; lists, dictionaries and sets can.

questions.question: What does "data"[1:3] return?
questions.explanation: Slicing starts at index 1 and stops before index 3, so it takes the characters at 1 and 2: "a" and "t".

questions.question: Which line opens a file so it is closed even if an error happens?
questions.explanation: A with block closes the file when the block ends, whether it ends normally or with an error.

questions.question: Which command shows the line-by-line changes you have not staged yet?
questions.explanation: git diff with no arguments compares your working files with what is staged. git log lists commits.

questions.question: What does git pull do?
options: Fetches the remote branch and merges it (or rebases) into yours
Uploads your commits to the remote
questions.explanation: git pull is git fetch followed by a merge, or a rebase if you set it so. git push uploads.

questions.question: You need to undo a commit that is already on a shared branch. The safe choice is…
options: Delete the branch and start again
questions.explanation: git revert adds a new commit that undoes the old one, so nobody else's history is rewritten.

questions.question: Which file lists the paths Git should not track?
questions.explanation: .gitignore lists files and folders Git leaves out, such as build output and local secrets.

questions.question: Which command shows running processes and their CPU use, updating live?
questions.explanation: top shows processes sorted by CPU use and refreshes every few seconds. htop is a friendlier version where installed.

questions.question: What does chmod 644 report.txt allow?
options: The owner reads and writes; everyone else only reads
Everyone reads, writes and runs it
Only the owner can run it
questions.explanation: Each digit is owner, group, others. 6 is read and write, 4 is read only.

questions.question: Which command finds the lines containing "error" in app.log?
questions.explanation: grep prints the lines of a file that match a pattern. find looks for files by name or type.

questions.question: What does cd .. do?
questions.explanation: Two dots mean the parent folder. cd on its own, or cd ~, goes home.

questions.question: What is the difference between an image and a container?
options: They are two names for the same thing
An image is a read-only template; a container is a running copy of it
A container is a template; an image is what runs
Images run only on Linux; containers run anywhere
questions.explanation: You build an image once and can start many containers from it, each with its own writable layer.

questions.question: Which file describes how to build an image?
questions.explanation: A Dockerfile lists the steps to build an image. A compose file describes how to run several containers together.

questions.question: What does docker run -p 8080:80 nginx do?
options: Port 80 on your machine reaches port 8080 in the container
It starts two containers, one on each port
It runs nginx on port 8080 inside the container
Port 8080 on your machine reaches port 80 in the container
questions.explanation: The -p option is host port first, then container port.

questions.question: Files a container writes outside any volume…
options: Are kept forever on the host
Are lost when the container is removed
Are shared with every other container
questions.explanation: A container's own layer goes with the container. Data that must stay goes in a volume or a bind mount.

questions.question: Which HTTP method should only read and never change anything on the server?
questions.explanation: GET is a safe method: it asks for data. POST, PATCH and DELETE change things.

questions.question: Which status code usually answers a POST that created something?
questions.explanation: 201 says something new was created, often with a Location header pointing at it.

questions.question: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
options: 401: you aren't allowed; 403: we don't know who you are
Both mean the server is down
Both mean the page doesn't exist
401: we don't know who you are; 403: we know, and you aren't allowed
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized asks for valid credentials. 403 Forbidden means the credentials are fine but the action isn't allowed.

questions.question: Which method should have the same effect whether it is sent once or twice?
questions.explanation: PUT replaces a resource with what you send, so repeating it changes nothing more. Two POSTs can create two records.

questions.question: What does continuous integration mean?
options: Releasing once a quarter after a long test phase
Merging small changes often, with an automatic build and tests on each one
Writing the tests after the release
Everyone working on one shared server
questions.explanation: CI finds problems early because every change is built and tested as soon as it is pushed.

questions.question: Tests fail in the pipeline on a pull request. What usually happens?
options: The merge is blocked until the tests pass
It merges anyway and is fixed later
The repository is locked for everyone
questions.explanation: Branch protection makes a passing pipeline a condition for merging, so broken code stays out of the main branch.

questions.question: Where should a password or deploy key used by a pipeline be kept?
options: In the repository, next to the code
In the CI system's secret store
questions.explanation: Secret stores keep the value out of the code and the logs and let you change it without a commit.

questions.question: Continuous delivery and continuous deployment differ how?
options: Deployment has the manual step; delivery is automatic
Delivery keeps every change ready to release with a manual step; deployment releases every passing change automatically
questions.explanation: Both build and test every change. Continuous deployment also releases it without a person pressing a button.

questions.question: Five salaries in lakh: 3, 4, 4, 5 and 50. Which number describes a typical salary best?
questions.explanation: The median, 4, isn't pulled up by the one very high salary. The mean, 13.2, is.

questions.question: What is the median of 2, 7, 4, 9 and 5?
questions.explanation: Sorted, the values are 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, and the middle one is 5. 5.4 is the mean.

questions.question: A test gives a p-value of 0.03. What does that mean?
options: There is a 3% chance there is no effect
We are 97% sure the result matters
If there were no real effect, results at least this extreme would come up about 3% of the time
questions.explanation: A p-value is about the data assuming no effect. It is not the chance the effect is real, and it says nothing about size.

questions.question: Two measures have a correlation of 0.9. What does that show?
questions.explanation: A correlation close to 1 means a strong straight-line link. It says nothing on its own about cause.

questions.question: Which function finds a value in the first column of a table and returns a value from another column of that row?
questions.explanation: VLOOKUP looks down the first column. XLOOKUP and INDEX with MATCH do the same job more flexibly.

questions.question: The formula =A1*$B$1 is copied down a column. Which part stays the same?
questions.explanation: Dollar signs fix the column and the row, so $B$1 stays put while A1 becomes A2, A3 and so on.

questions.question: Which tool summarises sales by region and month without writing formulas?
questions.explanation: A PivotTable groups and totals rows by the fields you drag in, and updates when you refresh it.

questions.question: What does =COUNTIF(A:A, ">100") return?
options: The total of the values above 100
How many cells in column A are above 100
TRUE if any value is above 100
questions.explanation: COUNTIF counts the cells that meet the condition. SUMIF would add them up.

questions.question: A city column holds "Mumbai", "mumbai " and "MUMBAI". What do you do first?
options: Trim the spaces and make the case the same
Replace them with the most common city
Leave them; they mean the same
questions.explanation: Left as they are, they count as three cities in any group or chart. Trimming and one case make them one.

questions.question: 2% of rows have no age. What is a sensible first step?
options: Find out why they are missing, then choose to drop or fill them
Leave them out of the report without saying so
questions.explanation: Whether values are missing at random decides what is safe. Zero would pull every average down.

questions.question: Two rows are the same in every column, including the order id. They are most likely…
options: A duplicate to check and remove
questions.explanation: An id is meant to be unique, so a repeated row with the same id is usually loaded twice. Check the source before deleting.

questions.question: An order date column mixes 03/04/2026 and 2026-04-03. What is the risk?
options: 03/04 can be read as 3 April or as 4 March
questions.explanation: Day and month order differs by country. Convert every date to one format, such as 2026-04-03, before you work with them.

questions.question: Which chart shows monthly revenue over two years most clearly?
questions.explanation: A line chart shows change over time. Pie and donut charts show parts of one whole.

questions.question: Which chart compares sales across 8 product categories best?
questions.explanation: Bars of one length scale are easy to compare. Eight pie slices are hard to tell apart, and 3D makes it worse.

questions.question: A bar chart's value axis starts at 90 instead of 0. What does that do?
options: Makes the chart easier to print
Makes the differences look bigger than they are
questions.explanation: Bar length should match the value, so bar charts start at zero. A cut axis exaggerates small gaps.

questions.question: To see how ad spend relates to sales across 200 shops, use…
questions.explanation: A scatter plot puts one dot per shop, so you can see a trend, clusters and odd shops at a glance.

questions.question: Which AWS service stores files as objects in buckets?
questions.explanation: S3 is object storage. EC2 runs servers, RDS runs managed databases and Lambda runs functions.

questions.question: Which AWS service gives you virtual servers?
questions.explanation: EC2 instances are virtual machines you choose the size and system of.

questions.question: What is IAM used for?
options: Deciding who can do what in your AWS account
questions.explanation: IAM holds users, roles and policies. Route 53 does DNS, SES sends email.

questions.question: What is the safest way to let an app on EC2 read from S3?
options: Put access keys in the app's code
Attach an IAM role to the instance
questions.explanation: A role gives the instance short-lived credentials that change on their own, with no keys to leak.

questions.question: How would you check whether a string has all unique characters, and what is the time cost?
questions.strongCovers: A set or fixed-size array giving O(n) time, compared with the O(n log n) sort approach and its space trade-off.

followUps.text: How would you do it without any extra data structure?
What changes if the string can hold any Unicode character?

questions.question: Explain the difference between an array and a linked list, and when you would pick each.
questions.strongCovers: Indexed access versus cheap insertion and deletion, memory layout and cache use, with a fitting example for each.

followUps.text: Which would you use for a queue that grows and shrinks a lot, and why?
How does a dynamic array grow, and what does that cost on average?

questions.question: How would you find two numbers in an array that add up to a target value?
questions.strongCovers: A hash map pass in O(n) time, or the two-pointer method on a sorted array, with the trade-offs explained.

followUps.text: What if the array is already sorted and you cannot use extra memory?
How would you return every pair instead of just one?

questions.question: What is the difference between breadth-first and depth-first search on a graph?
questions.strongCovers: Queue versus stack or recursion, level-by-level versus deep paths, and BFS giving shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

followUps.text: Which one would you use to find the fewest hops between two cities, and why?
How do you avoid visiting the same node twice?

questions.question: What is Big-O notation, and what is the time cost of binary search?
questions.strongCovers: Growth rate as input size rises, worst case focus, and O(log n) for binary search on sorted data.

followUps.text: Why does binary search need the data to be sorted?
Give an example of an O(n squared) approach you have improved.

questions.question: Explain the four pillars of object-oriented programming with an example.
questions.strongCovers: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism, each tied to a small concrete example rather than definitions only.

followUps.text: Which of the four do you use most in your own code, and where?
When can inheritance make code harder to change?

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
questions.strongCovers: Shared state and partial implementation versus a contract only, multiple interfaces, and when to choose each.

followUps.text: Give a case where you would use both together.
How have default methods changed this in recent Java versions?

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
questions.strongCovers: Same name with different parameters at compile time versus a subclass replacing behaviour at run time.

followUps.text: Which one gives run-time polymorphism, and how does the program decide which method to call?
Can a static method be overridden?

questions.question: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?
questions.strongCovers: Looser coupling, easier change and testing, avoiding deep hierarchies, with an example such as a car having an engine.

followUps.text: Show how you would change an inheritance design into one using composition.
When is inheritance still the right choice?

questions.question: Design the classes for a simple parking lot system.
questions.strongCovers: Clear classes such as ParkingLot, Level, Slot, Vehicle and Ticket, sensible responsibilities and relationships, and room to extend.

followUps.text: How would you add support for electric vehicle charging slots?
How would you find the nearest free slot quickly?

questions.question: What is a unit test, and how is it different from an integration test?
questions.strongCovers: Testing one small piece in isolation versus several parts working together, with speed and scope differences.

followUps.text: Give an example of a bug that only an integration test would catch.
How many of each kind would you aim for in a typical service?

questions.question: What are mocks and stubs, and when do you use them?
questions.strongCovers: Replacing slow or external dependencies, stubs returning fixed data, mocks checking interactions, and not over-mocking.

followUps.text: What can go wrong when a test mocks too much?
Name the mocking library you have used and one thing it does well.

questions.question: How would you write unit tests for a function that calculates a discount based on order value?
questions.strongCovers: Normal cases, boundary values at each threshold, invalid inputs, and clear test names using arrange-act-assert.

followUps.text: Which boundary values would you test, and why?
How would you test it if the discount rules came from a database?

questions.question: What is test-driven development, and what are its pros and cons?
questions.strongCovers: Writing a failing test first, then code, then refactoring, with better design and coverage traded against early speed.

followUps.text: Describe the red, green, refactor cycle in your own words.
When would you not use TDD?

questions.question: What does code coverage tell you, and what does it not tell you?
questions.strongCovers: Which lines ran during tests, not whether the assertions are meaningful, and why 100% coverage is not the goal.

followUps.text: What coverage target would you set for a new service, and why?
How else would you judge whether tests are good?

questions.question: What is the difference between == and equals() in Java?
questions.strongCovers: Reference comparison versus value comparison, String examples, and overriding equals together with hashCode.

followUps.text: Why must hashCode change when you override equals?
What happens with == on two Integer objects holding 127 and 128?

questions.question: How does a HashMap work internally?
questions.strongCovers: Hashing keys to buckets, handling collisions with lists or trees, resizing at the load factor, and key immutability.

followUps.text: What happens when two keys land in the same bucket?
Why should keys be immutable?

questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
questions.strongCovers: Compile-time enforced handling versus runtime exceptions, examples of each, and when to throw which.

followUps.text: Give an example of each from code you have written.
Why do many teams avoid checked exceptions in new code?

questions.question: How do you make a class immutable in Java?
questions.strongCovers: Final class and fields, no setters, defensive copies of mutable fields, and why immutability helps with threads.

followUps.text: How would you handle a field that holds a List?
Name one immutable class from the Java standard library.

questions.question: What are Java streams, and when would you use them instead of a loop?
questions.strongCovers: Declarative pipelines with map, filter and collect, readability, laziness, and cases where a loop is clearer.

followUps.text: Write a stream that returns the names of employees earning above a value, sorted.
What is the risk of using parallel streams?

questions.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
questions.strongCovers: Function versus block scope, hoisting, reassignment rules, and const not making objects immutable.

followUps.text: What does the temporal dead zone mean?
Why can you still change an object declared with const?

questions.question: Explain how the event loop works in JavaScript.
questions.strongCovers: Single thread, call stack, task and microtask queues, and why promises run before setTimeout callbacks.

followUps.text: In what order would a promise callback and a setTimeout of zero run, and why?
How can a long loop freeze a web page?

questions.question: What is a closure, and where have you used one?
questions.strongCovers: A function keeping access to its outer scope after that scope ends, with a practical example such as a counter or event handler.

followUps.text: How can closures cause a memory leak?
Explain the classic loop problem with var and closures.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
questions.strongCovers: Type coercion versus strict comparison, surprising examples, and defaulting to ===.

followUps.text: Give one surprising result of using ==.
When, if ever, would you use ==?

questions.question: How do promises and async/await help with asynchronous code?
questions.strongCovers: Avoiding nested callbacks, chaining, error handling with catch or try/catch, and running tasks in parallel with Promise.all.

followUps.text: How would you run three API calls in parallel and wait for all of them?
What happens if you forget to await a promise?

questions.question: What is the difference between a pointer and a reference in C++?
questions.strongCovers: Nullability, reassignment, syntax, and when each is the clearer choice in function parameters.

followUps.text: When would you pass by const reference instead of by value?
Can a reference be null?

questions.question: What is RAII, and why is it important in C++?
questions.strongCovers: Tying resource lifetime to object lifetime, destructors releasing resources, and examples such as smart pointers and locks.

followUps.text: How do smart pointers use RAII?
What problem does RAII solve when an exception is thrown?

questions.question: What is the difference between unique_ptr and shared_ptr?
questions.strongCovers: Single versus shared ownership, reference counting cost, and the risk of cycles with shared_ptr.

followUps.text: How do you break a reference cycle between two shared_ptr objects?
Why should you prefer make_unique over new?

questions.question: What is a virtual function, and how does it work?
questions.strongCovers: Run-time polymorphism through a base class pointer, the vtable idea, and virtual destructors in base classes.

followUps.text: Why should a base class with virtual functions have a virtual destructor?
What is a pure virtual function?

questions.question: How would you choose between a vector, a list and a map in the STL?
questions.strongCovers: Contiguous storage and fast index access, cheap insertion in the middle, and sorted key lookup, with typical use cases.

followUps.text: What happens to iterators when a vector grows?
When would you use unordered_map instead of map?

questions.question: What are goroutines, and how are they different from operating system threads?
questions.strongCovers: Lightweight, runtime-scheduled functions with small growable stacks, many goroutines on few threads, and started with the go keyword.

followUps.text: How would you wait for ten goroutines to finish before continuing?
What happens to running goroutines when main returns?

questions.question: How do channels work in Go, and when would you use a buffered channel?
questions.strongCovers: Typed pipes for passing values between goroutines, blocking send and receive, buffers to decouple producer and consumer speed.

followUps.text: What happens if you send on a channel that nobody reads from?
How does select help when reading from several channels?

questions.question: How does error handling work in Go compared with exceptions?
questions.strongCovers: Errors as returned values checked with if err != nil, wrapping with fmt.Errorf and %w, errors.Is and errors.As, and panic only for bugs.

followUps.text: How would you add context to an error while keeping the original error checkable?
When is it acceptable to use panic?

questions.question: What is an interface in Go, and how does a type satisfy one?
questions.strongCovers: Method sets satisfied implicitly with no implements keyword, small interfaces such as io.Reader, and accepting interfaces in function parameters.

followUps.text: Why are small interfaces like io.Reader considered good Go style?
What is the empty interface, and what replaced most of its uses?

questions.question: How would you build a simple REST API in Go using the standard library?
questions.strongCovers: net/http handlers, routing, JSON encoding and decoding, status codes, and graceful shutdown with context.

followUps.text: How would you stop a slow request from running forever?
How would you test a handler without starting a real server?

questions.question: What is the difference between a class and a struct in C#?
questions.strongCovers: Reference type on the heap versus value type copied on assignment, when structs fit small immutable data, and boxing costs.

followUps.text: What happens when you pass a struct to a method and change it inside?
What is boxing, and why can it slow code down?

questions.question: How do async and await work in C#?
questions.strongCovers: Tasks representing work, await freeing the thread while waiting on I/O, avoiding .Result and .Wait, and async all the way down.

followUps.text: Why can calling .Result on a task cause a deadlock?
What is the difference between Task.WhenAll and awaiting tasks one by one?

questions.question: What is dependency injection in ASP.NET Core, and what are the service lifetimes?
questions.strongCovers: Registering services in the container, constructor injection, and the transient, scoped and singleton lifetimes with an example of each.

followUps.text: What goes wrong if a singleton depends on a scoped service?
How would you swap a real email service for a fake one in tests?

questions.question: What is LINQ, and what is the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable?
questions.strongCovers: Query syntax over collections, in-memory evaluation versus translation to SQL, and deferred execution.

followUps.text: Why can calling ToList too early make a database query slow?
Write a LINQ query that groups orders by customer and sums the totals.

questions.question: How does garbage collection work in .NET, and when do you need IDisposable?
questions.strongCovers: Generational collection of managed memory, and releasing unmanaged resources such as files and connections with Dispose and using.

followUps.text: What does a using statement do for a database connection?
What are the generations in the .NET garbage collector?

questions.question: Which data structure gives O(1) average time for checking whether an item exists?
questions.explanation: A hash set looks items up by their hash in constant time on average. A sorted array needs O(log n) binary search, and a linked list or heap needs a scan.

questions.question: Which principle hides an object's internal data behind methods?
questions.explanation: Encapsulation keeps fields private and exposes behaviour through methods, so internal data can change without breaking callers.

questions.question: A unit test calls a real payment gateway over the network. What is the main problem?
options: It is slow and can fail for reasons outside the code
It makes the test too short
questions.explanation: Network calls make tests slow and flaky. Unit tests should replace external services with stubs or mocks.

questions.question: Which collection keeps keys in sorted order?
questions.explanation: TreeMap stores keys in a red-black tree, so they stay sorted. HashMap keeps no order, and the lists are not key-value maps.

questions.question: What does typeof null return in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: typeof null returns "object" because of a long-standing quirk in the language. Check for null with === null instead.

questions.question: Which smart pointer allows only one owner of an object?
questions.explanation: unique_ptr has sole ownership and can only be moved, not copied. shared_ptr allows many owners, and auto_ptr is removed from modern C++.
